## How to Choose a 3PL for D2C India

To choose a 3PL for D2C India, compare providers on warehouse location, inventory accuracy, COD and returns handling, technology integrations, service levels, and the full cost per order. The cheapest storage quote is rarely the best decision if dispatch errors, delayed returns, or poor reconciliation reduce your margins.

India's 3PL market has kept expanding alongside the country's D2C boom. Estimates of the market's 2026 value vary widely by methodology — roughly USD 25-38 billion depending on the research firm — but every major forecast agrees the direction is up, with e-commerce cited as a primary driver as the sector is projected to grow roughly five-fold to around USD 300 billion by 2030. That growth has brought more fulfillment providers, more warehouse networks, and more overlapping service claims into the market, which makes a structured evaluation more useful today than it was a few years ago, not less.

A third-party logistics provider, or 3PL, stores your products, processes orders, packs parcels, hands them to carriers, and often manages returns. For an Indian D2C brand, the right 3PL can make growth easier. The wrong one can create stock mismatches, customer complaints, cash-flow gaps, and avoidable replacement costs.

This guide explains how to evaluate 3PL fulfillment providers in India before signing a contract. If your fulfillment questions are really about the ecommerce website and order data itself rather than the warehouse floor, our piece on [WooCommerce's 2026 order-storage changes](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-woocommerce-hpos-2026) covers that side of the stack.

## Understand What You Need From a 3PL

Many D2C founders begin by asking, “What is the per-order charge?” That is useful, but it is not the first question. First define the work you need the provider to perform.

Some brands need only storage and pick-and-pack. Others need inward quality checks, kitting, gift wrapping, marketplace dispatches, COD reconciliation, reverse logistics, and regulatory support for specific product categories.

### Typical 3PL fulfillment services

A provider may offer some or all of the following:

- Receiving inventory from manufacturers or importers
- Counting and checking incoming stock
- Bin or shelf storage
- Batch, lot, or expiry tracking
- Order processing from your online store
- Picking and packing
- Shipping label generation
- Courier allocation
- COD shipment handling
- Replacement shipments
- Return-to-origin processing
- Customer returns and quality checks
- Refurbishment, repacking, or liquidation
- Bundling and kitting
- Marketplace fulfillment
- Inventory reporting
- Cash-on-delivery reconciliation

Do not assume that every item is included in the advertised fulfillment charge. Services such as QC, inserts, fragile packing, branded packaging, return inspection, and storage of slow-moving stock may be billed separately.

### Map your current order profile

Prepare a simple operating brief before speaking to providers. Include:

- Product categories and SKU count
- Product dimensions and average weight
- Monthly order volume
- Peak-season order volume
- Percentage of prepaid and COD orders
- Main delivery states and cities
- Average number of items per order
- Expected return and RTO patterns
- Fragile, liquid, temperature-sensitive, or regulated products
- Packaging requirements
- Current sales channels
- Expected growth over the next year

You do not need perfectly accurate forecasts. A realistic range is more useful than an ambitious target. Separate normal monthly volumes from periods such as Diwali, festive sales, end-of-season promotions, and marketplace events.

### Decide what should remain under your control

A 3PL can manage physical operations, but you should retain visibility over stock, orders, returns, and cash. Decide in advance who will approve:

- Stock write-offs
- Damaged inventory classification
- Customer replacements
- Return acceptance
- Discounted sale of old stock
- Disposal of expired or unsellable goods
- Changes to packaging
- Courier service levels

A written responsibility matrix prevents disputes later.

## Choose the Right Warehouse Location

Warehouse location affects delivery time, shipping cost, customer experience, and the amount of stock you need to hold. There is no universally best location for every Indian D2C business.

A single warehouse near a major consumption market may suit a brand with concentrated demand. A brand shipping across India may eventually need more than one fulfillment location, but adding warehouses also increases inventory complexity.

### Consider demand concentration

Review where your recent orders came from. Group them by region or state and identify where a large share of customers are located. Consider whether the provider’s warehouses are close to:

- Your largest customer clusters
- Manufacturing or import points
- Courier and transport hubs
- Your office or quality team
- Return-heavy regions
- Your marketplace fulfillment requirements

For a brand based in Pune, a Maharashtra facility may be convenient for supervision and supplier coordination. However, a warehouse closer to customers in other regions may reduce transit distance or improve service for those orders. The decision should follow your order data, not just the warehouse’s advertised network.

### One warehouse versus multiple warehouses

| Model | Advantages | Limitations | Suitable when |
|---|---|---|---|
| One central warehouse | Easier stock control, simpler reconciliation, lower operational complexity | Longer delivery routes for some customers, possible higher shipping cost | Volume is moderate or demand is concentrated |
| Two or more regional warehouses | Faster regional dispatches, potentially better shipping economics | Stock must be split, replenished, and reconciled across locations | Demand is distributed and volume supports the complexity |
| 3PL network allocation | Access to multiple facilities without operating them yourself | More dependence on provider systems and allocation rules | You need broader reach but lack internal logistics capability |
| Supplier or factory dispatch | Lower storage requirement | Less control over packing, stock accuracy, and customer returns | Products are made or packed to order |

Ask how inventory is allocated between facilities. A warehouse network is not automatically useful if your best-selling SKUs are unavailable in the right locations.

### Check the physical facility

Request a warehouse visit, video walkthrough, or detailed facility documentation. Look for:

- Cleanliness and pest-control practices
- Fire-safety arrangements
- Access control and CCTV
- Racking and bin labelling
- Packing stations
- Separate areas for returns and damaged stock
- Moisture or temperature controls where needed
- Backup power and network connectivity
- Vehicle access and dispatch cut-off arrangements

A polished sales presentation does not confirm operating quality. Ask to see the actual area where your product category would be stored and packed.

## Evaluate Inventory Control and Warehouse Operations

Inventory accuracy is one of the most important parts of 3PL fulfillment. If the system says a product is available but the warehouse cannot find it, the result may be a cancelled order, a missed sale, or an unnecessary customer replacement.

### Ask how stock is received

Clarify the inwarding process:

- Does the warehouse count every unit or accept carton quantities?
- Are damaged units recorded at receipt?
- How are shortages and excess quantities reported?
- Can the provider capture batch numbers, manufacturing dates, and expiry dates?
- How soon does received inventory become available for sale?
- What documents are required for inwarding?
- Who is responsible for discrepancies between dispatch and receipt?

For products with expiry dates, ask whether the warehouse uses FEFO, or “first expiry, first out,” rather than only FIFO, or “first in, first out.” The correct method depends on your category and inventory policy.

### Review picking and packing controls

A reliable 3PL should have a clear process for locating the correct SKU and quantity. Ask whether workers use barcode scanning, paper lists, mobile devices, or a warehouse management system.

Important questions include:

- Is every SKU assigned a unique code?
- Are similar-looking products stored separately?
- Are barcode scans required at picking and packing?
- Can the system prevent dispatch of an unavailable SKU?
- Are photographs captured for selected high-value or fragile orders?
- How are inserts, samples, and promotional items added?
- How are fragile, liquid, or leakage-prone products packed?
- Can you specify different packaging rules by SKU?

If you sell multiple variants, such as colour, size, flavour, or pack quantity, variant-level accuracy is essential. A provider that performs well with simple single-SKU orders may struggle with bundles and multi-item carts.

### Define cycle counts and audits

Do not wait for an annual stocktake to discover differences. Ask about cycle counting, discrepancy investigations, and the procedure for correcting system stock.

Your agreement should explain:

- How often inventory is counted
- Who can request a recount
- How shortages are investigated
- How damaged stock is classified
- What evidence is needed for a claim
- Whether the 3PL is liable for unexplained loss
- How stock adjustments are approved

The purpose is not to penalise every small operational error. It is to ensure that both sides have a consistent and documented process.

## Assess Shipping, COD, Returns, and RTO Handling

D2C logistics in India requires more than handing parcels to a courier. Customers may request delivery changes, refuse COD parcels, return products after opening them, or report damage. These events affect the real cost of an order.

### Compare courier coverage, not only courier names

Ask which carriers the 3PL uses and how allocation is decided. The best courier for one PIN code may not be the best option for another. Review coverage for:

- Metro cities
- Tier-two and tier-three cities
- Remote and difficult-service PIN codes
- Jammu and Kashmir, the North-East, island territories, and other special areas where applicable
- Heavy, oversized, fragile, or liquid shipments
- Reverse pickups

Understand whether the 3PL uses direct courier contracts, a shipping aggregator, or a combination. Ask whether you can select or exclude certain carriers based on service history.

### Understand COD processes

COD can help customers who do not prefer online payment, but it creates additional operational requirements. Ask:

- How are COD amounts reconciled?
- When are remittances made?
- Is reconciliation done by order, shipment, or settlement file?
- How are short remittances handled?
- Who follows up on delayed settlements?
- What happens when a COD order is partially delivered or refused?
- Are courier COD charges separate from fulfillment charges?

Your finance team should be able to match orders, shipments, delivery status, and settlements without relying on manual spreadsheets alone.

### Examine returns and RTO separately

A customer return is not the same as a return-to-origin shipment. In a customer return, the parcel is sent back after delivery. In an RTO, the shipment returns because it was not delivered, often due to refusal, an incorrect address, or repeated failed attempts.

Ask how the provider handles:

- Return request creation
- Reverse pickup
- Return quality inspection
- Resalable and non-resalable stock
- Product exchanges
- Replacement orders
- Missing accessories or packaging
- Damaged returns
- RTO inwarding
- Refund or store-credit status updates

For apparel, footwear, cosmetics, food, and other categories, return inspection rules can be very different. Document what counts as acceptable stock before the first return arrives.

## Check Technology and Integrations

Technology should reduce manual work and make problems visible. It should not simply add another dashboard that your team rarely uses.

### Core integrations to examine

Depending on your business model, the 3PL may need to connect with:

- Shopify or WooCommerce
- Magento or another commerce platform
- Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, or other marketplaces
- Shiprocket, Pickrr, NimbusPost, or similar shipping tools
- Payment gateways
- Accounting or enterprise resource planning software
- Customer-support systems
- WhatsApp or email notification systems

Ask whether the connection is a standard integration, a file exchange, or a custom API. Also ask who pays for setup, customisation, maintenance, and future changes.

### Inventory and order visibility

At minimum, you should be able to see:

- Available inventory
- Reserved inventory
- Damaged or blocked stock
- In-transit stock
- Orders received
- Orders on hold
- Orders packed
- Orders dispatched
- Delivered orders
- RTO and return status
- Reconciliation exceptions

Clarify how frequently data is updated. “Real time” can mean different things in practice. Ask what happens if an order is placed while the warehouse system or integration is unavailable.

### Data ownership and security

Your customer and order data remains important even when fulfillment is outsourced. Review:

- User access controls
- Login and permission management
- Data export options
- Backup arrangements
- Incident reporting
- Data retention after termination
- Use of customer information by subcontractors
- Restrictions on using your data for other purposes

India’s Digital Personal Data Protection framework may be relevant depending on the information processed and the role of each party. Have your legal or compliance adviser review the contract where personal data is involved. The 3PL agreement should clearly define responsibilities rather than relying on general assurances.

## Compare the Commercial Model Properly

3PL pricing in India can include several components. Compare the total operating cost, not only the headline pick-and-pack fee.

### Common cost components

You may encounter charges for:

- Storage by pallet, bin, cubic volume, or occupied space
- Inwarding and unloading
- Pick-and-pack
- Packaging material
- Branded packaging
- Inserts, samples, and kitting
- Courier and freight
- COD handling
- Reverse logistics
- RTO processing
- Quality checks
- Relabelling or barcoding
- Inventory counts
- Special handling
- Technology or integration
- Minimum monthly billing
- Peak-season labour or storage
- GST

Ask for a sample invoice based on your own product mix. A per-order quote without assumptions is difficult to compare.

### Ask about billing assumptions

Request written answers to questions such as:

- Is the fulfillment charge per order or per item?
- Is a multi-item order charged once or by each picked unit?
- How are split shipments billed?
- Is storage charged on occupied space or a fixed allocation?
- Is there a minimum monthly commitment?
- Are packaging materials included?
- Are courier charges based on actual or volumetric weight?
- How are weight disputes handled?
- Are return and RTO charges different?
- Does the price change during sales events?
- Are rates revised annually or when volume changes?
- Is GST added to all applicable services?

Volumetric weight can materially affect shipping cost for lightweight products in large boxes. Ask for the formula used and the process for challenging incorrect weight measurements.

### Review the contract, not only the proposal

The agreement should cover:

- Scope of services
- Service levels
- Billing and payment terms
- Inventory ownership
- Loss and damage liability
- Insurance responsibilities
- Confidentiality and data handling
- Subcontracting
- Audit and inspection rights
- Dispute resolution
- Notice period
- Exit assistance
- Stock removal process
- Treatment of unpaid invoices
- Rate revision rules

Do not accept a vague promise that all issues will be “resolved mutually.” Define how an issue is reported, investigated, credited, and closed.

## Check Compliance and Category-Specific Requirements

Your 3PL should support your compliance process, but it cannot replace your responsibility as the seller or brand owner.

### GST and movement documentation

Discuss how stock movements and invoices will be handled across states. Depending on your structure and transaction, GST registration, place-of-supply rules, tax invoices, stock transfers, and e-way bill requirements may apply.

Ask the provider:

- Which entity receives and stores your goods?
- How are inter-state stock transfers documented?
- Who generates shipping documents?
- Can the system support your GSTIN and invoice format?
- How are cancelled orders and credit notes reflected?
- Who retains proof of delivery and dispatch records?

Get advice from your tax professional for your specific structure. A 3PL may provide system functionality, but tax treatment depends on your business and transaction model.

### Product-specific obligations

Requirements vary by category. Examples include:

- FSSAI-related controls for food products
- Legal Metrology declarations for packaged goods
- Batch and expiry tracking for relevant products
- Product and label requirements for cosmetics
- Special handling or documentation for medicines and medical products
- Battery, electronics, or hazardous-material restrictions
- Import and customs documentation for imported inventory

Confirm whether the provider has handled products similar to yours. Ask for the storage, labelling, and dispatch controls that apply to the category rather than accepting a general “we handle everything” answer.

### Packaging and environmental considerations

Packaging affects damage rates, customer perception, shipping cost, and waste. Decide whether the 3PL will use your materials, source standard materials, or manage both.

Clarify:

- Approved box and mailer sizes
- Plastic or paper packaging options
- Tamper-evident requirements
- Product protection standards
- Disposal of damaged packaging
- Use of recycled or recyclable material
- Responsibility for packaging compliance where applicable

If your products are prone to leakage or breakage, test actual packed parcels before launch.

## Use Service Levels and a Pilot Before Committing

A proposal and a warehouse tour are not enough. Test the provider with a controlled pilot.

### Set practical service levels

Your service-level agreement may cover:

- Inwarding time after stock receipt
- Order processing cut-off times
- Pick-and-pack accuracy
- Dispatch accuracy
- Inventory accuracy
- Return inspection time
- Response time for support tickets
- COD reconciliation timelines
- Damage and loss reporting
- System uptime or incident communication

Avoid choosing targets that cannot be measured. Define the data source, review period, exclusions, and remedy if the service level is missed.

A service level is useful only when you receive regular reporting. Ask for a monthly operations review covering orders, exceptions, returns, stock variances, ageing inventory, and open disputes.

### Run a pilot with real complexity

A pilot should include more than your easiest SKU. Include:

- Single-item orders
- Multi-item orders
- Bundles
- COD and prepaid orders
- Fragile or special-packaging items
- Address corrections
- Cancellations
- Customer returns
- RTO parcels
- A marketplace order if relevant

Measure the time from order receipt to dispatch, accuracy of picking, quality of packing, status updates, and ease of resolving exceptions. Also check whether your team can understand the dashboard and reconcile the reports.

### Speak with current or recent customers

Ask the provider for references that resemble your business in category, volume, and complexity. Do not rely only on large enterprise references if you are a small D2C brand.

Useful questions include:

- How quickly are issues acknowledged?
- Are inventory discrepancies resolved with evidence?
- Are invoices easy to verify?
- Does the provider communicate during peak periods?
- How difficult is it to retrieve stock or change providers?
- Are promised integrations working in daily operations?

The provider may not disclose confidential information, but it should be able to explain its standard processes clearly.

## Common Mistakes When Selecting a 3PL

Several mistakes appear repeatedly in D2C fulfillment decisions.

### Choosing only on the lowest rate

A lower pick-and-pack fee may be offset by expensive packaging, storage minimums, return charges, or higher error rates. Compare cost per successfully delivered order and cost per resalable returned unit, not just cost per dispatch.

### Selecting a network that is too complex

Multiple warehouses can improve coverage, but splitting inventory without reliable demand planning can create stockouts in one location and excess stock in another. Start with an operating model your team can monitor.

### Ignoring peak capacity

Ask what happens during festive demand, marketplace events, product launches, and promotional campaigns. Confirm labour availability, dispatch cut-offs, storage limits, and courier capacity during those periods.

### Treating returns as an afterthought

Returns affect inventory, refunds, customer support, and accounting. Define the process before launch, including quality grading and timelines.

### Accepting manual work without controls

Spreadsheets may be workable at a very small scale, but manual uploads and reconciliations introduce avoidable errors as order volume grows. If manual steps are necessary, document approvals and reconciliation checks.

### Failing to plan the exit

You should be able to move inventory, customer data, and operational records to another provider if necessary. Confirm notice periods, stock removal charges, data exports, and final reconciliation before signing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does a 3PL do for a D2C brand in India?

A 3PL typically stores inventory, picks and packs orders, arranges shipping, and manages some part of returns and COD operations. The exact scope varies, so the service list and exclusions should be written into the agreement.

### Should a small D2C brand use a 3PL?

A 3PL can be useful when order handling is taking time away from product, marketing, or customer service work, or when stock and dispatch errors are increasing. It may be better to begin with a flexible provider and a limited pilot rather than commit to a large warehouse network immediately.

### How many warehouses should an Indian D2C brand use?

There is no fixed number. Base the decision on order geography, shipping economics, inventory value, replenishment capability, and the operational complexity your team can manage.

### Is COD still important for Indian D2C fulfillment?

COD remains relevant for some customer segments and product categories, but it creates additional reconciliation and RTO work. Compare prepaid and COD performance using your own order data, and ask the 3PL for a clear process for settlements, refused deliveries, and RTO stock.

### What should be included in a 3PL contract?

The contract should cover services, rates, storage, packaging, service levels, inventory liability, returns, data handling, insurance, billing, subcontracting, termination, and exit support. It should also explain how disputes over weight, stock shortages, damages, and invoices will be investigated.

### Can a 3PL integrate with Shopify and marketplaces?

Many providers support common commerce platforms and marketplaces, but integration quality differs. Confirm whether your required channels are supported, how inventory is synchronised, how cancellations are handled, and what happens when the connection fails.

## Where to Start

Begin with your last few months of order data. Prepare a one-page brief covering SKU count, product dimensions, monthly and peak orders, COD share, delivery regions, return patterns, packaging requirements, and sales channels.

Shortlist providers that have experience with your product category and target customer geography. Compare warehouse conditions, inventory controls, courier options, technology, full landed fulfillment cost, and contract terms. Then run a pilot using real orders before moving all inventory.
